entry.content:
Advertising

Levi's Yeti Roars Atop the Week's Best Campaigns

With Midi Health, e.l.f. Beauty, Visit Iceland and Columbia Sportswear

by David Gianatasio
November 5, 2026
12:00 pm
2 min read
Share:

This week’s best work, ranked by the Clios’ staff, features two impressive stop-motion campaigns and other excellent efforts. But nothing beats a Yeti, especially for the festive season.

Bestie: A Claymation Yeti Stomps Through Levi’s Holiday Campaign

This beast gets a sweet character arc. He starts out gruesome and destructive. Will he cough up some bucks for smashing through the cabin wall? Probably not. But a Levi’s sweater puts him in the mellowest yuletide mood. Superb Claymation stylings from Blinkink. Read More

2. Top Comics Michelle Buteau, Jessica Kirson and More Roast Menopause for Midi Health

The notion of “roasting’ menopause itself might sound like a stretch. But these performers deliver a show that’s hilarious and on point. If you want to start a cultural convo about potentially touchy topics, laughter can provide the best way in. Read More

3. Alan Cumming Narrates e.l.f.’s Animated Holiday Spot

The Shadow agency and Apartment D director Cami Kwan help the brand convey a heartfelt message that packs more whimsical imagery than you can fit beneath a tree. Yet, it also feels grounded in reality, with Alan Cumming working his Scottish pipes for a warm and winning V.O. Read More

4. Who Needs AI Notetakers? Visit Iceland Offers ‘Knittakers’ Instead

Real Icelanders from across the Nordic nation will take your place on video calls and knit brief summaries for your pleasure. M+C Saatchi developed the initiative, which stitches tech, old-school craft and odd humor into an attractive tapestry. Or maybe a sweater. Read More

5. Columbia Sportswear’s Bunker Helps You Survive the Apocalypse in Rugged Style

And the prize for best performance by a CEO in a bunker goes to Columbia’s Tim Boyle. Who wouldn’t want a 40 ft. x 8 ft. steel container brimming with gear and grub buried in their backyard? From Adam&Eve\TBWA and Smuggler director Benji Weinstein. Read More

entry.title: The U.K. Holiday Ads Have Arrived: John Lewis, Aldi, Tesco and More
entry.summary: Advertising The U.K. Holiday Ads Have Arrived: John Lewis, Aldi, Tesco and More Plus good cheer from Asda, Argos and Sainsbury's by Shahnaz Mahmud November 5, 2026 8:00 am 4 min read Share: The holiday ad season is well underway in the U.K., with commercials dropping every day th
entry.content:
Advertising

The U.K. Holiday Ads Have Arrived: John Lewis, Aldi, Tesco and More

Plus good cheer from Asda, Argos and Sainsbury's

by Shahnaz Mahmud
November 5, 2026
8:00 am
4 min read
Share:

The holiday ad season is well underway in the U.K., with commercials dropping every day this week. Below, Muse looks at some of the notable entries so far. Classic themes abound, with brands leaning into familiar tropes and timeless tales to conjure the Xmas spirit.

John Lewis, ‘Don’t Give Up on Giving’

This marks the retailer’s 20th holiday campaign. Dame Kristin Scott Thomas shares the stage with a vintage Fisher-Price Snoopy-style toy. When Scott Thomas’ grandchildren arrive for the holidays, the kids aren’t impressed with the pooch. When she opts to put cash in an envelope to satisfy their holiday appetites, the doggo speaks up, telling her she can do better than that. Next, a magical neon pedicab whisks them away to a John Lewis store for a shopping spree. Back home, the kids are treated to a room filled with magical lights and disco balls. Naturally, they dance on with their grandma. A version of The Rolling Stones’ “You Can’t Always Get What You Want” adds a rocked-up vibe. Saatchi & Saatchi led the creative. 

Argos, “Tales of Argos Past”

Here, Argos riffs on Charles Dickens‘ A Christmas Carol. BAFTA-winning actor and comedian Richard Ayoade is visited by The Ghost of Christmas Presents and the Dinosaur of Argos Past. They transport him back to his childhood and, when they question what made him so gruff as an adult, Richard replies: “Life and despair.” They explain that, in his youth, he never got past the toy section, and then reveal all of the high-tech gadgets Argos sells in the here and now. At last, Richard comes to understand the error of his ways, leading to a happy Christmas Day. Declan Lowney of Merman directed, with T&P handling creative.

Sainsbury’s, ‘The Big Delivery’

The supermarket reimagines the world of Roald Dahl, focusing on The BFG—his 1982 novel featuring “The Big Friendly Giant.” Down with a bad cold, The BFG decides to forgo Christmas. But his human friends Annie and Fred deliver him a holiday feast. The spot, which uses live action and animation, puts the friends in peril en route in their car. Antics with a giant mouse, a king-sized cheese platter and Brussels sprouts follow. When they arrive safely, they proclaim: “No one should miss Christmas!” The push was created by New Commercial Arts, while Rogue Films handled production. Electric Theatre Collective oversaw visual effects. 

Tesco, ‘Because the Wrong Address’

The supermarket chain pulls at the heartstrings with a story about a long-ago friendship that went awry. Lizzie had a food delivery order sent to a previous address. Goodhearted Polly offers to meet her halfway. It becomes clear they were friends in the past, but the relationship soured. Lizzie gives an abrupt thanks and waves Polly off, but her car won’t start. Polly comes to the rescue and drives her old friend home. Will the tale end happily? Perhaps around a dinner table set with goodies from Tesco. Will it!? BBH London created the work. 

Asda, ‘All of Christmas at Asda Price. BOOM!’

The grocer opts for a highly stylized Christmas epic, showcasing food, home decor and more. The tale morphs from a family gathering at the dinner table—with Asda low-low price tags near some of the items—to a party featuring the mum riding on a giant Christmas cracker among dancing toy soldiers. BOOM! indeed. From Lucky Generals.

Aldi, Teaser: ‘The Search for Cauli-Dog’

The grocer carries beloved characters forward for its 2026 ad offer. Here, we get a tease of things to come. Aldi puts Kevin the Carrot at the center once again. He and his daughter Chantenay are putting up missing posters for their Cauli-Dog. Clues will trickle in from Aldi, keeping the suspense going. McCann Manchester helped develop the campaign.

entry.content:
Advertising

Chewy Joins the Stop-Motion Avalanche

Is this the doggone cutest holiday campaign of the year?

by David Gianatasio
November 4, 2026
9:15 am
4 min read
Share:

And now for something completely different: A stop-motion holiday campaign.

The parade of animated fare continues with Chewy joining e.l.f. and Levi’s via three shorts developed with Starburns and director David Shafei.

Unlike the other two brands, Chewy blends stop motion and live action to bridge the gap between real-life and a snowy fantasy world. Its iconic blue delivery box serves as a portal, natch. Ratcheting up the cuteness, real doggos and their puppet doppelgängers appear.

The pooches, snowmen, mice, pine trees, a penguin, a cat and more were handcrafted from needle-wool over wire armatures. Their faces and body language are sweet and expressive. Some might find the approach too adorbs for its own good. But such grumps deserve coal in their stockings.

Next, the brand hypes its “Chewy Claus” program that helps support pet adoptions at participating shelters nationwide:

Wisely, these vignettes tell simple tales. They’re imminently snackable, but packed with great details that merit repeat viewings.

Yes, there’s a risk of stop-burnout this festive season—and we’re just a few days into November. Still, these efforts have all been top-notch so far. And Chewy’s initiative feels nostalgic without getting too Rankin-Bassy. Which is to say it’s pleasingly familiar but also stands out, thanks in large part to the puppetry replacing Claymation.

Also of note: the trend of brands self-consciously eschewing AI in favor of traditional creative techniques. This approach has become synonymous with dedication to craft, conveying notions of human attention to detail and quality. Fair enough. But AI’s here to stay; its one more tool in adland’s kit. One wonders how long marketers—which automate various processes left and right—will continue to trumpet their artisanal leanings before the point becomes moot (or even starts to feel regressive).

“We want to capture a little bit of what pets feel when they see a Chewy box,” Shafei explains in the BTS reel below. “We’re trying to blend the magic of the holiday with the magic of our pets. And I just can’t think of a better way to bring that through than stop-motion animation.”

Here, Muse chats with Chewy chief brand officer Melissa Bell about the strategy:

What was the inspo here?

The idea stems from imagining what a dream holiday world would look like to our pets. For five years, Chewy Claus has brought magic to pets during the holidays by delivering gifts and fulfilling big and small wishes. A Santa Claus for pets was something they could only dream of before Chewy Claus existed and these TV spots delve deeper into what else our pets dream of for the holidays. Whether that’s a forever home, a new cozy bed, their favorite treats or playing in the snow with their furry best friends.

Who is the target audience—current customers? Looking for new ones?

The target is always pet parents. When they see these ads, we want them to experience the nostalgia and joy from the holiday classics we know and love, but through their pets eyes and remember Chewy has everything they need to make their pets holiday season special.

No AI anywhere—right?

Correct. Every detail was thoughtfully crafted by professional artists and craftspeople, with no AI-generated visuals used in the production. Our customers have always appreciated the personal, one-of-a-kind touches they receive from Chewy, whether it’s receiving a hand-painted pet portrait, a heartfelt birthday card or a condolence gift after losing a pet. We believe in the power of connecting through real, human interactions.

Lots of cute animated Xmas ads—this year more than ever. Why will yours stand out?

We have some pretty cute talent in our spots! Before Graham was the star of our Chewy Claus spot, he was an actual rescue dog looking for a family. And the other puppets are inspired by real animals as well. We believe combining the real pets with the Chewy dream world version of themselves makes the creative not only adorable, but also memorable.

entry.summary: Advertising Columbia Sportswear's Bunker Helps You Survive the Apocalypse in Rugged Style It's a 'Don't Panic Room.' So try to maintain your composure by David Gianatasio October 30, 2026 10:00 am 4 min read Share: If civilization suddenly implodes, you’ll want to rock gear with
entry.content:
Advertising

Columbia Sportswear's Bunker Helps You Survive the Apocalypse in Rugged Style

It's a 'Don't Panic Room.' So try to maintain your composure

by David Gianatasio
October 30, 2026
10:00 am
4 min read
Share:

If civilization suddenly implodes, you’ll want to rock gear with a spiffy logo when you emerge into the post-apocalyptic wilderness.

To that end, Columbia Sportswear steps up to the end-times challenge with a “Don’t Panic Room” contest that features a steel shipping container tricked out like a survivalist’s kitschy, branded dream. Along with loads of Columbia jackets, they packed tools, utensils, cots, a chemical toilet and tins of food (including “Some Kind of Meat”) into the 40 ft. x 8 ft. space. It won’t sit rusting in your back yard or driveway, because Columbia will pay for you to actually bury the thing.

You get a robo-dog for companionship, too. Perhaps it can parlay with near-future kill-bots annihilating any humans that remain. Good boy!

CEO Tim Boyle stars in an amusing promo below from Adam&Eve\TBWA and Smuggler director Benji Weinstein.

“Since the beginning of time, people have predicted the end of the world,” he says. “I don’t really buy into all that stuff. But since Columbia protects helps protect you from nature’s worst, we figure, ‘Better safe than sorry.'”

“Those tech bros already have their bunkers,” Boyle continues. “But they don’t have the skills to survive outdoors. Try starting a campfire with crypto. Or fly-fishing with microchips. Good luck with that.”

The competition invites folks to send videos displaying their survival skills for a chance to win. That grounds the stunt in Columbia’s consumer community, acknowledging their fans’ dedication to hiking, foraging, navigation and all manner of sweaty wilderness activities.

“We want to reward the real survivalists and outdoors people who appreciate what Mother Nature has to offer,” says brand marketing chief Matt Sutton.

Columbia accepts entries through Nov. 24. In addition to the hero clip, the initiative features Silicon Valley billboards and influencer support.

Below, agency creative William Cottam and James Crosby break down the strategy.

What was the inspo here?

We kept seeing stories about Silicon Valley tech bros building themselves elaborate bunkers. Which got us thinking, what’s the point of having a bunker if you don’t have the skills to survive outside it? So we thought it’d be funny if Columbia gave one away to someone who actually knows what they’re doing. You know, someone who could actually keep humanity going.

Why a survival room specifically?

Columbia has been engineering gear to protect people from Mother Nature for nearly 90 years. So building something to protect you from absolutely everything felt like a pretty natural, if slightly ridiculous, extension of that. It’s “Engineered for Whatever” taken to its logical extreme. Even if that extreme is an ice age, a meteor taking out the power grid or whatever sends us all running for the hills.

Who’s the target audience and why will it appeal to them?

Anyone who loves the outdoors and reckons they could survive with more than a smartphone and a decent Wi-Fi connection. We wanted to celebrate genuine outdoor skills rather than the size of someone’s bank account. And, frankly, who wouldn’t want to win a bunker?

I like how this transcends ad creative. It feels so tactile and real.

That’s what we love about it, too. We didn’t want to just make an ad about a bunker. We wanted to actually build the bloody thing. There’s something wonderfully ridiculous about creating a fully functioning 40-foot survival bunker, filling it with Columbia gear and delivering it to someone’s home. Columbia’s even agreed to give the winner $35,000 to help bury the thing underground. I mean, that’s commitment. Let’s just hope the winner has a spare 8 ft. x 40 ft. patch of land lying around.

Nice CEO performance, too.

Tim comes to the table with his own ideas, like the dog pooping bolts at the end. That was all him. And he was more than happy to get behind the wheel of a semi-truck too. He genuinely has fun with it all, which makes our jobs a lot easier.

Here’s our roundup of the week’s Top 5, chosen by the Clios’ staff.

Bestie: It’s OK to Be a Hot Mess Sometimes, Maruchan Says

Maruchan feels you, Gen Z. And they made the cheeky wearables to prove it. Spent all your money at the bar? That’s what your T-shirt says. Ah well, at least you’ve got those Saucy Noods to savor. Developed with Goodby Silverstein & Partners and Beyond Studios’ creative director Cole Poska. Read More

2. Public Storage Tapped 4 Indie Filmmakers to Spin Terrifying Tales

What’s in those containers? Brand-boosting terror, that’s what! Microdramas are all the rage, and these vids from The Infinite Agency deliver a potent combination of thrills and chills for Spooky Season. Spoiler: That Teddy Bear ain’t right. See the trailer below. Read More and See All the Shorts Here

3. Walmart Reimagines ‘The Muppet Christmas Carol’ With Walton Goggins as Scrooge

Walton Goggins’ yuletide range is pretty impressive. After a winning turn as Walmart’s Grinch last year, he plays Ebenezer Scrooge in a musical, Muppet-y take on the holidays for 2026. Great spirit (heh) and production values from Fallon and director Randall Einhorn. Read More

OK, who wants to sit on Giant Puppet Santa’s lap? An oddly compelling early Xmas morsel from Bob Baker Marionette Theater, artist Jimmy Marble and digital creator Jillian Wheeler (who directed). Read More

entry.title: An Inside Look at Hoorae’s ‘Parental Advisory’ Reveals the Twists and Turns of Making Microdramas
entry.summary: Advertising An Inside Look at Hoorae's 'Parental Advisory' Reveals the Twists and Turns of Making Microdramas Muse visits the set to learn how brands and producers navigate the hottest trend in storytelling by T.L. Stanley October 28, 2026 1:45 pm 7 min read Share: The clock is t
entry.content:
Advertising

An Inside Look at Hoorae's 'Parental Advisory' Reveals the Twists and Turns of Making Microdramas

Muse visits the set to learn how brands and producers navigate the hottest trend in storytelling

by T.L. Stanley
October 28, 2026
1:45 pm
7 min read
Share:

The clock is ticking in the final hours of a seven-day shoot, and the summer sun is beating down on a rented Los Angeles bungalow that serves as a backdrop for the microdrama “Parental Advisory.”

Sometime after high noon, tragedy strikes, threatening to derail the project’s tight turnaround. One of the show’s stars is feeling dizzy and lightheaded from the triple-digit temperatures. Paramedics arrive as the cast and crew sweats, literally and figuratively.

“No one could’ve predicted a heat wave or a heat stroke,” said Dzifa Yador, head of digital at producer Hoorae. “And this impacts our no. 1 on the call sheet.”

After a health check on the ailing actor, the decision comes down: She needs to stop filming, even though she has pivotal scenes and promotional vignettes with brand partner e.l.f. Cosmetics to complete.

Can this production be saved?

Pins and Needles

The cliffhanger is catnip—foundational, even—to the multibillion-dollar vertical series industry. In this case, the pins-and-needles development wasn’t scripted. It happened, though it took place behind the scenes rather than in the content itself.

A bit of life imitating art in a burgeoning genre that shrinks the classic TV soap opera into binge-worthy, bite-sized bits for a mobile audience. Relying heavily on exaggerated tropes and over-the-top twists, it gives viewers the dopamine hits that keep them coming back for more episodes. Think Pringles: once you pop, you can’t stop.

Skipping right to the spoiler: The actor rallied and returned to set the next day, wrapping up the work right on schedule. Like the layered intrigue in “Parental Advisory,” everything resolves in the end.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by HOORAE, An Issa Rae Company (@hooraemedia)

Microdrama Machine

“Parental Advisory,” which dropped its 50-episode run on Oct. 28, comes from Issa Rae’s Hoorae as part of an ongoing deal with TikTok that brings exclusive series to the platform and its PineDrama app.

The relationship kicked off in April with “Screen Time,” a techno-thriller that instantly went viral, racking up 620 million global views and counting.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by HOORAE, An Issa Rae Company (@hooraemedia)

The second project, a 68-episode reality-dating show a la Temptation Island called “The Compatibility Experiment,” debuted Oct. 14, logging 110 million views so far.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by HOORAE, An Issa Rae Company (@hooraemedia)

And now there’s “Parental Advisory,” a whodunnit about bougie prep school families where it’s the grownups, not the kids, who’ve gone wild.

The three projects, in quick succession, are just the beginning. For 2027, Hoorae and TikTok plan to release a new microdrama every four to six weeks, each with brand financing and integration, according to Yador.

Muse got a peek into the making-of “Parental Advisory,” which churned out roughly an hour’s worth of entertainment with a fraction of the manpower, time and budget of a traditional Hollywood venture.

“We shoot 13-15 pages a day with one camera team, about 45 in the crew, seven in the cast—everything is as skeleton as it can be,” Yador said. “We have one or two takes to get what we need, and then we move on.”

Brand Backed, Not Brand Stacked

Even under those constraints, Hoorae Media and its sister company Ensemble are striving for premium-level storytelling.

“We’re making these series for audiences first,” said Ian Schafer, Ensemble’s president and co-founder with Rae. “They’re not commissioned by brands. But we’re bringing brands in, integrating them in ways that feel natural.”

General Mills, with its Gushers candy, appeared in “Screen Time.” Alt soda Poppi and Sol de Janeiro perfumes cameoed in “The Compatibility Experiment.” e.l.f. has exclusivity in “Parental Advisory.” The brands enjoy active and passive placement, low-key enough not to trigger algorithms or get labeled “branded content.” The ad partners are disclosed.

“We don’t prioritize product over story—we do the opposite,” said Yador, noting that brand backing means the content is free for consumers to watch, where paywalls are common in the space. Brands that collaborate with Hoorae and Ensemble get an early look at the microdrama scripts and can share ideas. Their reps are invited to the set to oversee the brand’s face time. And they’re on hand IRL when the cast shoots themed vignettes that do “a lot of the heavy lifting” in cementing the sponsorship, Schafer said.

A global ambassador from e.l.f. trained the stylist and makeup artist on “Parental Advisory,” and brand execs made sure an actor applied her bronzer and blush just-so during key scenes. (Brushes and strokes are everything).

Execs at e.l.f. were looking for “natural moments” in entertainment content instead of old-school product placement. “It’s all about being part of the storytelling, not interrupting it,” said Patrick O’Keefe, chief integrated marketing officer at e.l.f. Brands.

Microdramas were definitely on the radar for a brand that’s dabbled in mockumentaries, comedy shorts and other unconventional marketing meant to serve its loyalists and cultivate new customers.

“We’ve seen the power microdramas have with subcultures, and the impact Hoorae’s first series had was undeniable,” O’Keefe said. “When we looked at ‘Parental Advisory,’ we saw an organic way for e.l.f. to show up within a story our community would already be watching and talking about.”

Kitsch Is King

China may have birthed the microdrama, and remains the largest market globally for the snacky entertainment. But the U.S. has caught the bug. At its schlockier end, there are blockbusters like “My Gorgeous Wife Is an Ex-Convict,” “Never Divorce a Secret Billionaire Heiress” and the trend-right “Seducing My Hockey Rival.”

TechCrunch said the genre “feels like Cocomelon for adults,” and ad agency Walrus summed it up like this: “Think of the cheesiest thing you’ve ever seen on Lifetime and cut its budget by 80 percent—that’s a microdrama.”

Yet female millennials are passionate fans, part of an audience that spends more minutes a day with microdramas than with Netflix or Disney+, per Walrus. Short-drama apps like ReelShort, DramaBox and others reported 850 million downloads in Q1 2026, a 140 percent year-over-year leap.

TikTok recently signed its second microdrama deal with Made By Us Studios for creator-led vertical series, while legacy media has taken notice, with NBCUniversal, BET, A&E and Fox all announcing their entry into the space.

AI slop has arrived, not surprisingly, but Hoorae is committed to human talent with union memberships on all fronts. “We’re taking a more craft-driven approach,” Schafer said, noting that Hoorae’s projects aim to break new talent and champion diverse voices.

Edge of the Seat

Appointment viewing, in the traditional sense, is a relic these days, replaced with what Schafer calls “pass the time with” content. That’s where microdramas like “Parental Advisory” come in, offering high-concept 60-second episodes filled with lust, revenge, dark comedy and hyperbolic hijinks that make waiting in line at CVS a bit less painful.

The show, which brought back much of the crew from Hoorae’s previous vertical series, colors outside the lines in its true crime template (romance is the genre’s bread and butter). Producers study what’s fueling views, shares and convos across pop culture. Predictably, horror is on the future docket.

Back at the “Parental Advisory” set, director Kendall Outing runs through a scene with actor Raél Ba, searching for the right reaction when her character catches her straying husband on a mysterious phone call.

“Shimmy to the left, please, then give it a beat and cock your head,” Outing says, acting it out himself and advising against anything “too sitcom-y.”

Ba nails the “gotcha” moment, giving fellow actor Henderson Wade an appropriate jump scare.

Will this couple survive? Who else is cheating, in the bedroom and the boardroom, in this viperous social-climbing circle? And who gets bludgeoned at the fancy gala? The answers await here, one addictive minute at a time.

entry.content:
Ad of the Week

It's OK to Be a Hot Mess Sometimes, Maruchan Says

Serving up merch that gets what you're going through

by Shahnaz Mahmud
October 28, 2026
1:00 pm
2 min read
Share:

In a bid to entice Gen Z, Maruchan’s Saucy Foods is acknowledging that being a hot mess is a part of its DNA.

The maker of instant Ramen and lunch noodles has partnered with Beyond Studios’ creative director Cole Poska—known for his spins on branded merch—to devise a platform that includes clothing and a media campaign. Goodby Silverstein & Partners handled creative development.

The wearables include T-shirts and accessories that give fans permission to own their oft-messy lives. They sport lines like: “Spent all my money at the bar, at least I have Saucy Noods” and “I’m a hot mess with Saucy Noods.”

The impetus arose from fans creating their own Maruchan designs. 

“That inspired us to give fans a (brand-sanctioned!) merch line in collaboration with iconic designer Space Boy Cole,” says Charlotte Cordova, director of communication strategy at GS&P. “The campaign centers on how Saucy Noods are there for you in your hot-mess moments. We’re showing up with activations that position Saucy Noods as the go-to food for those moments: on social, in AI responses, in rideshare apps and now with a merch line.”

“We told Cole that everything we made for this line should support people in their moments of mess, so it made sense to include things like a Hot Mess hoodie, under-eye patches and a migraine mask,” adds creative director Kate Baynham. “Maruchan will be there for you no matter what.”

The merch is available for a limited time in Maruchan’s TikTok Shop.

The campaign can be seen on Snapchat ads that run after 9 p.m., via Uber ads that land after 7 p.m. and in partnership with TikTok show Are You Okay?, which celebrates people’s messy lives.

entry.summary: Advertising Walmart Reimagines 'The Muppet Christmas Carol' With Walton Goggins as Scrooge Following his epic turn as the Grinch from last year by Christine Champagne October 28, 2026 10:30 am 5 min read Share: Walton Goggins is back as the face of Walmart, this time stepping int
entry.content:
Advertising

Walmart Reimagines 'The Muppet Christmas Carol' With Walton Goggins as Scrooge

Following his epic turn as the Grinch from last year

by Christine Champagne
October 28, 2026
10:30 am
5 min read
Share:

Walton Goggins is back as the face of Walmart, this time stepping into the role of Ebezener Scrooge in a film inspired by The Muppet Christmas Carol. Riffing on that classic holiday flick, the spot finds Goggins surrounded by Kermit the Frog, Miss Piggy, The Great Gonzo, Rizzo the Rat and Pepé the King Prawn.

If you are a fan of Brooklyn Nine-Nine, you will get a kick out of seeing Stephanie Beatriz, beloved in the role of grumpy detective Rosa Diaz, as Scrooge’s cheerful niece. Kudos to the casting director for making this choice.

Directed by Randall Einhorn of Radical Media, the film launches Walmart’s broader “A Who Knew Carol” campaign. Through a series of videos and social content, the seasonal push finds the famously crotchety Scrooge discovering the plethora of gifts the retailer has to offer.

Here, Fallon CEO Nikki Baker discusses how Walmart’s association with Goggins—who suited up as the Grinch in a Walmart Black Friday campaign last year—benefits the brand. She also delves into the making of the hero film.

Why is Walton Goggins a great rep for the brand? And what was it like seeing him as Scrooge?

Walton brings so much energy and dedication to everything he does. He has become a true partner to our team over the last year and a half. He genuinely loves the work that we’ve been doing, and that passion comes through on the screen. Seeing him step into Scrooge was amazing because he brought depth and warmth to the role. He played Scrooge with real human emotion, which made his transformation and his rapport with the Muppets genuine and so much fun to watch.

The hero film is quite a production. Can you tell me about the thinking behind it as well as the campaign in general? 

The Muppet Christmas Carol is a masterclass in reappraisal—it’s all about taking a second look. At the end of the day, we wanted to build a fun holiday story that’s entertaining while also authentically bringing Walmart in. The musical numbers are a critical piece to what makes the original a fan favorite. We wanted to honor the fandom by kicking off the campaign with a musical number similar to the film. This Walmart-inspired number kicks off the season by launching “A Who Knew Carol” and establishing the universe, before we roll into a continuous campaign across the coming months that spotlights brand-name gifts, Black Friday savings and Express Delivery.

What was the biggest challenge in making the hero film?

Ensuring we were honoring the original Muppet classic while making sure the film delivered on Walmart’s business goals. The production was built on physical sets full of Easter eggs nodding to the original film and new music. Standing on set with Walton and the cast, seeing the incredible detail in every prop and costume, made all the magic.

Why was Randall Einhorn the right director to bring it to life? 

Randall has an incredible background in comedy and TV, so he knew exactly how to direct big performances and keep the story moving. He handled our hero broadcast and OLV films brilliantly. At the same time, our social video content was directed by SARBY, which is made up of Sara Cummings and Abby Gross, two of our creative directors at Fallon. They brought a fast, digital and culture-first perspective that made the social assets feel just as engaging as the musical film. 

I loved seeing the two old guys from the balcony as the ghosts.

We couldn’t do this without bringing back Statler and Waldorf, who played the Marley brothers in the original, and their signature heckling energy is perfect for our NFL spots. Across the whole campaign, every Muppet had a specific role to play. We brought in classic favorites, new Muppets and created our very own Muppet [a blue Walmart bag called Bagsy who appears in other videos but not the hero video], all with a goal to honor the original story while celebrating the holidays with Walmart.  

How did you incorporate gifts into the film and into the campaign in general? I love the teeny tiny lava lamp Pepé the King Prawn is holding.

Gifts can definitely sit in the background, but we prefer bringing them naturally into the story. We think it’s an incredible creative challenge, and we want to share the breadth of the gift assortment at Walmart. Whether it is a high-end De’Longhi espresso maker or a funny little detail like that tiny lava lamp, we wanted every product to feel like an authentic part of the scene.

This film is spirited and fun. Do you especially enjoy bringing big holiday stories like this to life? 

The secret to a lot of our work has been what we like to call “cultural commerce.” If people are entertained, they really do want to interact with your brand. It’s always great getting to build a story that people actually want to follow along with throughout the season. When you start with a great brand like Walmart and then bring together an amazing cast, real physical craft and iconic characters like The Muppets, it starts to feel like genuine entertainment. The campaign is festive, funny, and, hopefully, a fun break in the middle of a busy season.

entry.summary: Advertising Public Storage Tapped 4 Indie Filmmakers to Spin Terrifying Tales 'Don't Watch' microdramas for Halloween. (That's just the title. They want you to watch) by David Gianatasio October 27, 2026 9:30 am 3 min read Share: So, people pack away unspeakable horrors in self-s
entry.content:
Advertising

Public Storage Tapped 4 Indie Filmmakers to Spin Terrifying Tales

'Don't Watch' microdramas for Halloween. (That's just the title. They want you to watch)

by David Gianatasio
October 27, 2026
9:30 am
3 min read
Share:

So, people pack away unspeakable horrors in self-storage units these days. We’d suspected as much.

Such facilities serve as springboards for “Don’t Watch,” a quartet of unsettling micro-tales from Public Storage and The Infinite Agency. Unlike Yahoo’s somewhat similar Halloween offering, which spoofed Hollywood tropes for laughs, this frightful foursome plays it straight with the chills and suspense.

So, if you like skeletal remains, creepy mannequins, unlucky charms and breathless chases through dark woods that you know won’t end well … you’re kind of weird.

Which is awesome. Because this stuff’s for you.

Here’s a trailer that offers disturbing glimpses of what lies behind those roll-up doors:

Now, let’s look at the full tales, which run for a few minutes each. First, Emmy-winner Brandon Walker presents a collection of dusty, crusty remains that should have been left for dead:

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Found TV (@watchfoundtv)

Next, writer-director Elaine Frost wonders if grandma will “still be there.” Unfortunately, in the end, we find out.

@publicstorage 02_FOREVER_YOUNG.MP4 Content by: @Deep Red Perfect Blue ♬ original sound – Public Storage

In our third installment, from Eric Orange, we learn why taking an unreliable 51-year-old truck on a cross-country trek during Spooky Season is a freakishly bad idea.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Eric Orange (@ericorangedotcom)

“We wanted to make something scary that didn’t feel like an ad. Public Storage were great partners,” Orange tells Muse. “They trusted us filmmakers to bring the thrills in an unexpected way. Love when brands listen to their audiences and aren’t afraid to take risks. If you’re going to be on social media as a brand, you should be having fun.”

Finally, our second ad this week with puppets in prominent roles. The first one featured merry Xmas marionettes. Jesse Blanchard’s “Teddy” poses a more sinister scenario:

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Puppetcore // Puppet Horror Films (@puppetcoreco)

“Storage can be a very mundane industry. That’s why we love when brands like Public Storage are unafraid to make it fun and show off a personality rarely seen from their peers,” says agency ECD Tim McCarthy. “So, with the uprising of the horror genre, and the increase in popularity of longer-form content on social like microdramas, we thought Halloween was the perfect time to play up the spooky misconception about the service they offer.”

Remember: “These videos are scary—but storing your stuff with Public Storage never is.” (But if you watch these and decide to just keep cramming mementos in the attic, who can blame you?)
